monosaccharide.short: A single sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or galactose. The only form of carbohydrate the gut can absorb.

disaccharide.short: Two sugar units joined together: sucrose (table sugar: glucose + fructose), lactose (milk sugar: glucose + galactose) or maltose (glucose + glucose).

starch.short: The way plants store glucose: long chains of glucose units, found in bread, rice, pasta and potatoes. Digestion cuts it back to glucose.

dietary-fibre.short: Carbohydrate chains from plants that our own gut enzymes can't split, so they aren't absorbed in the small intestine. Gut bacteria in the large intestine ferment part of them.

sglt1.short: The transporter that moves glucose and galactose from the gut into the cells lining it, carried along with sodium. It can be saturated when a lot of glucose arrives at once.

glut5.short: The transporter that lets fructose into the cells lining the gut, by facilitated diffusion (downhill, no ATP). A separate door from the one glucose uses.

glut2.short: A glucose transporter on the blood side of the gut cells (and in the liver). It lets glucose, galactose and fructose leave the gut cell into the blood.

glycaemic-index.short: How much a food raises blood glucose over 2 h, as a % of the rise from the same amount of carbohydrate eaten as pure glucose. Low GI is 55 or less.

carbohydrate-loading.short: Eating a lot of carbohydrate (about 10–12 g per kg body mass a day) for 1–2 days while training little, to fill muscle glycogen above its normal level before a long race.

saturated-fat.short: Fat made of fatty acids with no double bonds in their carbon chain (common in butter, cheese and meat). The body can also make them itself.

unsaturated-fat.short: Fat made of fatty acids with double bonds in their chain: one (monounsaturated, as in olive oil) or two or more (polyunsaturated, as in fish oil and many seed oils).

maximal-fat-oxidation.short: The highest rate at which a person burns fat, in g·min⁻¹, measured in a graded test; it occurs at Fatmax. In athletes it averages about 0.6 g·min⁻¹.

protein-turnover.short: The constant breakdown and rebuilding of the body's proteins. Even when muscle size doesn't change, its proteins are being taken apart and remade.

net-protein-balance.short: Protein made minus protein broken down over a period. Positive: protein is being gained; negative: protein is being lost.

bcaa.short: Three amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) with a branched side chain. They are the amino acids muscle burns most during exercise.

urea.short: A small molecule the liver makes to get rid of the nitrogen from broken-down amino acids. It leaves the body in urine and sweat.

nitrogen-balance.short: Nitrogen eaten (in protein) minus nitrogen lost (urine, faeces, sweat). Positive means the body is gaining protein; negative means it is losing it.

carbohydrate-availability.short: Whether the carbohydrate eaten, and when, covers what the muscles and brain need for the training of the day (high) or falls short of it (low).

fuel-for-the-work-required.short: Planning carbohydrate intake session by session: more before and during hard or key sessions, less around easy ones.
